question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Everyone feels that he is pompous, but I know the underlying truth that he is a man of great understanding and love.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Modest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Pompous" means showing excessive self-importance or affected grandeur in behaviour, speech or appearance. (दिखावटी, घमंडी)
◦ Example: The pompous chairman insisted on being introduced with all his titles.

• Its antonym is "Modest", meaning having or showing a moderate estimate of one's own qualities or achievements; not boastful or arrogant. (विनम्र, सादा)
◦ Example: Despite winning the award, she remained modest about her achievement.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Lofty" (उच्च, गर्वीला): Means proud, haughty, or grandly imposing — this is actually close in meaning to "pompous", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Grandiose" (भव्यता दिखाने वाला): Means grand or impressive in a way that is meant to impress, or excessively grand — again a synonym of "pompous", not an antonym.

• Option 4: "Haughty" (घमंडी): Means arrogantly superior and disdainful — also a synonym of "pompous", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "pompous": pretentious, self-important, arrogant, ostentatious, bombastic.

• Other antonyms of "pompous": humble, unassuming, unpretentious, down-to-earth.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Suseptible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Susceptible", meaning likely to be influenced or harmed by a particular thing; easily affected.
◦ Example: Young children are highly susceptible to infections.

• Spelling key: SUS + CEPT + IBLE. The word contains a "c" after "sus" (sus-C-eptible) which is commonly dropped by mistake, producing the wrong spelling "Suseptible".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Souvenir" is correctly spelt — it means a thing kept as a reminder of a person, place or event.

• Option 2: "Symbolise" is correctly spelt — it means to be a symbol of, or to represent.

• Option 4: "Sympathetic" is correctly spelt — it means feeling or showing sympathy or understanding.

NOTE

• Other words where the silent/soft "c" is commonly dropped by mistake: "acceptable", "exceptional", "susceptibility", "reception".

• Always double-check words ending in "-ible" vs "-able" as SSC frequently tests this pair: susceptible, accessible, permissible, responsible take "-ible".

question:
Select the grammatically correct version of the following sentence.
He was youngest than his brother.
option_1: He was younger than his brother.
option_2: He was youngest to his brother.
option_3: He was too young than his brother.
option_4: He was young to his brother.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He was younger than his brother.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• When only two persons or things are compared, English uses the comparative degree of the adjective, formed with "-er" (for short adjectives), followed by the conjunction "than".

• Rule — Comparative Degree: Subject + verb + comparative adjective (adj + er) + than + the other person/thing.
◦ Example: Ravi is taller than Mohan.

• Applying the rule: since only two people (he and his brother) are being compared, the adjective "young" must take its comparative form "younger", followed by "than" — giving "He was younger than his brother."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because it drops the comparison altogether — the superlative form "youngest" is used only when comparing three or more things, and it should never be followed by "to".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "too young than" is an ungrammatical mix — "too" is never followed by "than"; "too" is followed directly by an adjective/infinitive (e.g. "too young to drive").

• Option 4 is incorrect because it removes the comparison entirely and wrongly uses "to" instead of "than", changing the meaning of the sentence.

NOTE

• Superlative degree (three or more things compared): adjective + "-est", e.g. "He is the youngest of the three brothers."

• Common SSC trap: using "than" with the superlative degree, or using the comparative degree without "than" — both are grammatically wrong.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
We were very much enthusiastic about our tour to Agra.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. casual.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Enthusiastic" means having or showing intense and eager enjoyment, interest, or approval towards something. (उत्साहित)
◦ Example: She was enthusiastic about joining the new project.

• Its antonym is "Casual", meaning showing a lack of interest, care, or concern; indifferent or relaxed about something. (लापरवाह, उदासीन)
◦ Example: He gave a casual reply, showing no real interest in the plan.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Obsessed" (जुनूनी): Means excessively preoccupied with something — this is actually closer in intensity to "enthusiastic", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Anxious" (चिंतित): Means feeling worried or nervous, which is a different emotion altogether and not a true opposite of enthusiastic.

• Option 4: "Inclined" (इच्छुक): Means having a tendency or preference towards something, which is still a form of positive interest — not an antonym of "enthusiastic".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "enthusiastic": eager, keen, passionate, zealous, avid.

• Other antonyms of "enthusiastic": apathetic, indifferent, unconcerned, half-hearted, blasé.

question:
Select the option that correctly expresses the following sentence in active voice.
This was talked about in the meeting by the officers.
option_1: The officers were talking about in the meeting.
option_2: The officers talked about this in the meeting.
option_3: The officers in the meeting had talked about it.
option_4: The officers talk about this in the meeting.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The officers talked about this in the meeting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "This was talked about in the meeting by the officers" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Past Tense (Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject).

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "by the officers" becomes the subject "The officers"; the past participle "talked about" takes its simple past form "talked about"; and the subject of the passive sentence "This" becomes the object.
◦ Active: The officers talked about this in the meeting.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "were talking about" is the past continuous form and also lacks an object after "about", making the sentence structurally incomplete.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "had talked about" is the past perfect tense, which changes the original simple past meaning of the sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "talk about" is in the simple present tense, whereas the original sentence is in the simple past tense.

NOTE

• When converting passive to active voice, always match the tense of the original passive sentence — only the subject/object and verb form change, not the tense itself.

• Common SSC trap: changing "was/were + V3" (simple past passive) into a present or perfect tense active sentence instead of simple past.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
From a recent research, evident is it that a lot more women have been opting for professional courses.
option_1: it is evident that more a lot women
option_2: it is evidently that a lot more women
option_3: it is evident that a lot more women
option_4: it is evidence that a lot more women
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. it is evident that a lot more women.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given segment "evident is it that a lot more women" has an incorrect, inverted word order. Standard English requires the structure "It is + adjective + that + clause" to introduce a fact.

• Rule: The anticipatory "it" must come first as the subject, followed by the linking verb "is", then the adjective ("evident"), and then the noun clause introduced by "that" — It + is + evident + that + clause.

• Also, the quantifier phrase must be "a lot more women" (a lot + more + noun), not "more a lot women", which is an incorrect word order.

• Applying the rule: "it is evident that a lot more women" correctly restores both the subject-verb-complement order and the correct quantifier order.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "more a lot women" wrongly orders the quantifier — it should be "a lot more women".

• Option 2 is incorrect because "evidently" is an adverb, but grammatically an adjective ("evident") is required after the linking verb "is", not an adverb.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "evidence" is a noun, and using it directly after "is" without an article ("is evidence that") is grammatically faulty in this construction; the required word is the adjective "evident".

NOTE

• The "It is + adjective + that" construction is a common SSC grammar pattern, e.g. "It is clear that...", "It is likely that...", "It is important that...".

• Distinguish: evident (adjective) = clearly seen/understood; evidently (adverb) = as is evident, apparently; evidence (noun) = the available facts indicating a belief is true.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the word 'Bleak' from the given sentence.
He looked gloomy, frail, broken and slow after the sudden demise of his brother.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. gloomy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Bleak" means cheerless, gloomy, dull and depressing; lacking hope or warmth. (उदास, निराशाजनक)
◦ Example: The future looked bleak after the factory shut down.

• Its closest synonym among the given options is "Gloomy", meaning dark, dismal, or sad in appearance or mood. (उदास, निराशाजनक)
◦ Example: The gloomy weather matched his gloomy mood.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Slow" (धीमा): Refers to lack of speed, an unrelated quality that does not match the meaning of "bleak".

• Option 3: "Frail" (कमज़ोर): Means physically weak or delicate, which describes physical condition, not a "bleak"/gloomy mood.

• Option 4: "Sudden" (अचानक): Means happening quickly and unexpectedly, referring to the manner of an event, not to a cheerless or dismal quality.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "bleak": dismal, desolate, grim, dreary, forlorn.

• Antonyms of "bleak": cheerful, bright, promising, hopeful.

question:
Select the correct spelling from the given options to fill in the blank.
Mihika was one of the ________ in the Master Chef competition held in our society last year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. contestants.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Contestants", meaning people who take part in a competition or contest.
◦ Example: All the contestants were given equal time to present their dishes.

• Spelling key: CONTEST + ANT + S. The word is formed from the root "contest" + the agent suffix "-ant" (one who does something) + the plural "-s".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Contextants" — incorrect; wrongly inserts an "x" from the unrelated word "context".

• Option 2: "Contestents" — incorrect; the suffix should be "-ants", not "-ents".

• Option 4: "Kontestants" — incorrect; the word begins with "C", not "K".

NOTE

• Related words: contest (verb/noun), contestant (noun), contestable (adjective).

• SSC frequently tests the "-ant" vs "-ent" suffix confusion, e.g. assistant, attendant, dependant vs. president, resident, correspondent — there is no fixed rule, so such words must be memorised individually.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Elusive
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Definite.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Elusive" means difficult to find, catch, achieve or define precisely; tending to evade description or grasp. (मायावी, दुर्बोध)
◦ Example: A lasting solution to the problem has remained elusive.

• Its antonym is "Definite", meaning clearly stated, precise, certain and free of ambiguity. (निश्चित, स्पष्ट)
◦ Example: She gave a definite answer without any hesitation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Explosive" (विस्फोटक): Refers to something likely to explode or a volatile situation — unrelated in meaning to "elusive".

• Option 2: "Affordable" (किफायती): Relates to reasonable price/cost, an unrelated quality.

• Option 4: "Rigid" (कठोर): Means unable to bend or change, describing stiffness, not a lack of clarity or difficulty of capture — not the true opposite of "elusive".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "elusive": evasive, intangible, indefinable, slippery, fleeting.

• Other antonyms of "elusive": clear, obvious, tangible, apparent, straightforward.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The students must complete the assignment by Friday.
option_1: The assignment must be completed by the students by Friday.
option_2: The assignment will be completed by the students by Friday.
option_3: The students will have completed the assignment by Friday.
option_4: The assignment must be complete by Friday by the students.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The assignment must be completed by the students by Friday.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The students must complete the assignment by Friday" uses the modal auxiliary "must".

• Rule — Passive voice with modal verbs: Subject + modal (must/can/should/may, etc.) + V1 + Object becomes Object + modal + be + V3 + by + Subject.

• Applying the rule: the object "the assignment" becomes the subject; the modal "must" is retained unchanged; "be" is added; the verb "complete" becomes the past participle "completed"; and "the students" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The assignment must be completed by the students by Friday.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "will be completed" drops the obligatory sense of the modal "must" and wrongly uses the future tense "will".

• Option 3 is incorrect because it keeps "the students" as the subject and uses "will have completed", which is an active, future perfect construction — not the passive form required.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "must be complete" uses the adjective "complete" instead of the past participle "completed", which is ungrammatical after "be" in the passive.

NOTE

• With modal verbs, the passive structure is always modal + be + V3, e.g. "can be done", "should be finished", "may be allowed".

• Never drop or change the modal verb itself when converting a modal-verb sentence from active to passive voice.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined group of words.
Kidney beans were boiled quickly when Nisha added a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed by the reaction itself.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. catalyst.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Catalyst" is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change. (उत्प्रेरक)
◦ Example: Platinum acts as a catalyst in many industrial chemical reactions.

• The underlined phrase — "a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed by the reaction itself" — is the precise dictionary definition of a catalyst.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Reactant" (अभिकारक): A substance that takes part in and is chemically changed/consumed during a reaction — the opposite of what is described, since a catalyst is NOT consumed.

• Option 3: "Enzyme" (एंजाइम): A biological catalyst made of protein; it is a specific type of catalyst found in living organisms, not the general term asked for here.

• Option 4: "Solute" (विलेय): The substance that is dissolved in a solvent to form a solution — unrelated to reaction speed.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often tested by SSC: inhibitor (a substance that slows down a reaction), reagent (a substance used to cause a chemical reaction, especially to test for another substance), solvent (the substance that dissolves a solute).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Sarah just gave ________ to a baby boy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. birth.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed expression "to give birth to" means to produce/deliver a baby.

• Rule: The idiomatic collocation is always "give birth to (a child/baby)" — this is a fixed phrase and no other word fits this construction with the same meaning.

• Applying the rule: "Sarah just gave birth to a baby boy" correctly conveys that Sarah has delivered a baby.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "breath" means the air taken into or expelled from the lungs; "gave breath" is not a standard collocation meaning delivery of a child.

• Option 3: "broth" means a thin soup, typically made from meat or vegetable stock; it is unrelated in both sound and meaning.

• Option 4: "berth" means a fixed bunk/sleeping place on a ship or train, or a job/position; it is a homophone-like word confused with "birth" but has an entirely different meaning.

NOTE

• Commonly confused word groups tested by SSC: birth/berth, breath/breadth — always check the meaning demanded by context, not just the sound of the word.

• Other fixed collocations with "birth": "date of birth", "birth certificate", "give birth to an idea" (figurative use).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
My mother asked my father to increase her personal use allowance.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. pin money.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Pin money" means a small sum of money for spending on inessential or personal items; personal/incidental expenses. (जेब खर्च, निजी खर्च के लिए थोड़ी रकम)
◦ Example: She works part-time just to earn some pin money.

• The underlined segment "personal use allowance" matches exactly this meaning of small, discretionary personal spending money.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Pell mell" (अस्त-व्यस्त, हड़बड़ी में): Means in a disorderly, hurried, confused manner.
◦ Example: The children ran pell mell out of the classroom.

• Option 2: "Rank and file" (आम लोग, साधारण सदस्य): Refers to the ordinary members of an organization, as opposed to its leaders.
◦ Example: The decision was unpopular with the rank and file of the party.

• Option 3: "Pins and needles" (सुन्न होना/बेचैनी): Means a tingling sensation in a limb, or a state of nervous anticipation.
◦ Example: She was on pins and needles waiting for her exam results.

NOTE

• Other money-related idioms often asked in SSC: "nest egg" (savings for the future), "a golden handshake" (a generous payment on leaving a job), "to foot the bill" (to pay for something).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Repeal
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Approval.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Repeal" means to officially revoke, cancel or withdraw (a law, decision or agreement). (रद्द करना)
◦ Example: The government decided to repeal the outdated tax law.

• Its antonym is "Approval", meaning the act of officially accepting, confirming or sanctioning something. (स्वीकृति)
◦ Example: The new bill received the approval of the entire assembly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Expense" (व्यय): Means the cost incurred in doing something — unrelated to cancellation or approval of a law.

• Option 3: "Separation" (अलगाव): Means the act of dividing or being divided — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: "Adversity" (विपत्ति): Means a state of hardship or misfortune — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "repeal": revoke, rescind, abolish, annul, nullify.

• Other antonyms of "repeal": enact, ratify, sanction, endorse, confirm.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
(O) on a regular basis can improve
(P) engaging in physical activity
(Q) the risk of chronic diseases, and boost mental health
(R) cardiovascular health, reduce
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. PORQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• To arrange jumbled parts correctly, first identify the subject of the sentence, then trace the logical chain of action and result.

• Part (P) "engaging in physical activity" is the gerund phrase that logically forms the subject of the sentence, so it must come first.

• Part (O) "on a regular basis can improve" naturally follows the subject, introducing the main verb "can improve" along with its qualifying phrase "on a regular basis".

• Part (R) "cardiovascular health, reduce" supplies the first object of "improve" ("cardiovascular health") and introduces the next verb "reduce".

• Part (Q) "the risk of chronic diseases, and boost mental health" completes the list of benefits, giving the object of "reduce" and the final verb phrase "boost mental health".

• Combining in the order P-O-R-Q: "Engaging in physical activity on a regular basis can improve cardiovascular health, reduce the risk of chronic diseases, and boost mental health."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (RPOQ) is incorrect because it begins with "cardiovascular health, reduce", which cannot logically open the sentence as it lacks a subject.

• Option 2 (PROQ) is incorrect because placing R directly after P ("engaging in physical activity cardiovascular health, reduce...") breaks the sentence, omitting the required verb "can improve".

• Option 4 (OQRP) is incorrect because it begins with "on a regular basis can improve", which has no subject to improve anything.

NOTE

• In parts-rearrangement questions, always look for the grammatical subject (often a gerund or noun phrase) to identify the starting part, and trace verbs and their objects/complements to build the logical chain.

• Watch for punctuation clues (commas, "and") — they usually mark the boundary between listed items, helping to fix the correct sequence.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A) to his neighbours
B) first name is Adam
C) that no one even
D) he is so rude
E) knows that his
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. D, A, C, E, B.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the pattern "so + adjective + that + clause" to express a result/consequence.

• Part (D) "he is so rude" naturally forms the opening main clause, introducing the subject "he" and the "so...that" construction.

• Part (A) "to his neighbours" logically follows "rude", since one is rude to someone.

• Part (C) "that no one even" introduces the result clause required by "so rude...that".

• Part (E) "knows that his" continues the result clause, and Part (B) "first name is Adam" completes it as the final clause.

• Combining in the order D-A-C-E-B: "He is so rude to his neighbours that no one even knows that his first name is Adam."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (B, D, A, C, E) is incorrect because it begins with "first name is Adam", which lacks a subject and does not make sense as an opening clause.

• Option 3 (A, C, B, D, E) is incorrect because it begins with "to his neighbours", which cannot start the sentence without the preceding clause "he is so rude".

• Option 4 (C, E, B, A, D) is incorrect because it begins with "that no one even", a subordinate clause that cannot open the sentence on its own.

NOTE

• The "so + adjective + that" construction always requires the main clause (with "so...adjective...") to precede the result clause introduced by "that".

• Similar constructions tested by SSC: "such a + noun + that", e.g. "It was such a hot day that we stayed indoors."

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
When I was in 5th grade, / I use to / ride on my / red bicycle.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. I use to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a habitual action in the past ("When I was in 5th grade") that no longer happens now, which requires the structure "used to", not "use to".

• Rule — "Used to" for past habits: Subject + used to + V1 is used to describe an action that regularly happened in the past but does not happen now. The form is always "used to" (with "d"), regardless of the subject.
◦ Example: I used to ride on my red bicycle when I was in 5th grade.

• The given segment "I use to" wrongly uses the base form "use" instead of the correct past habitual form "used".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "red bicycle" is grammatically correct — a simple adjective + noun phrase.

• Option 3: "When I was in 5th grade," is grammatically correct — a properly formed past-tense subordinate time clause.

• Option 4: "ride on my" is grammatically correct in context, correctly following "used to" with the base verb form.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "used to" (habitual past action) with "be/get used to" (accustomed to), e.g. "I am used to waking up early" (here "used to" is followed by a gerund, not a base verb).

• "Used to" never changes form for tense or subject — "He used to play", "They used to play" (never "useds to" or "use to" in past reference).

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom for the following statement.
The manager was punished for his negligence in work.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Bring to book.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Bring to book" means to make someone answer or account for their wrongdoing; to punish someone for a fault or offence. (सजा देना, जवाबदेह ठहराना)
◦ Example: The corrupt official was finally brought to book by the anti-corruption bureau.

• The given statement "The manager was punished for his negligence in work" matches exactly with being held accountable/punished for a fault — the meaning of "bring to book".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Bid defiance" (चुनौती देना): Means to openly resist or challenge someone/something.
◦ Example: The rebels bid defiance to the ruling government.

• Option 2: "Burn one's boats" (सारे रास्ते बंद कर लेना): Means to commit oneself irrevocably to a course of action, leaving no way to retreat.
◦ Example: By resigning from his job to start a business, he had burnt his boats.

• Option 3: "Bolt from the blue" (अप्रत्याशित घटना): Means a sudden and unexpected event.
◦ Example: His resignation came as a bolt from the blue for the team.

NOTE

• Other idioms of punishment/accountability often asked in SSC: "to pay the piper" (to bear the consequences of one's actions), "to face the music" (to accept punishment or criticism), "to get one's comeuppance" (to receive deserved punishment).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined segment in the following sentence.
As I walked through the old town, I couldn't help but feel a sentimental longing for the simpler times of my childhood.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. nostalgia.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Nostalgia" means a sentimental longing or wistful affection for the past, typically for a period or place with happy personal associations. (अतीत की यादों में डूबना)
◦ Example: Looking at the old photographs filled her with nostalgia.

• The underlined phrase "a sentimental longing for the simpler times of my childhood" is precisely the dictionary meaning of nostalgia.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Affection" (स्नेह): Means a gentle feeling of fondness or liking for someone, not specifically a longing for the past.

• Option 2: "Homesickness" (घर की याद): Means a longing for one's home while away from it — related but specifically about missing home, not the past in general.

• Option 3: "Inertia" (जड़ता): Means a tendency to remain unchanged or inactive — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other one-word substitutes related to memory/emotion often tested by SSC: reminiscence (the enjoyable recollection of past experiences), wistfulness (a feeling of vague or regretful longing), sentimentality (exaggerated feeling of tenderness/sadness).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Collection of written or spoken texts
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Corpus.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Corpus" means a collection of written or spoken texts, especially one compiled for linguistic study/analysis. (लेखों/भाषणों का संग्रह)
◦ Example: Linguists study a large corpus of texts to understand word usage patterns.

• The given phrase "collection of written or spoken texts" is the precise definition of a corpus.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Data bank" (आँकड़ा भंडार): Means a store of information, typically held on a computer — refers to data in general, not specifically written/spoken texts.

• Option 2: "Dictionary" (शब्दकोश): Means a reference book listing words and their meanings — not a collection of texts.

• Option 4: "Circa" (लगभग): Means "approximately" (used with dates), an entirely unrelated word (not even a noun referring to a collection).

NOTE

• Other one-word substitutes for collections often tested by SSC: anthology (a collection of poems/writings by different authors), archive (a collection of historical documents/records), compendium (a collection of concise information on a subject).

The entertainment (1)________ built by Walt Disney is sometimes called the ‘House of Mouse’ in acknowledgment of the leading role played by Disney's most famous creation, Mickey Mouse. Mickey's round mouse ears, either in silhouette or adorning a hat, have become one of the most (2)________ corporate logos in the world. But if a few business decisions in the 1920s had gone differently, they could have been rabbit ears.

In the mid-1920s Disney was a young (3)________ producing a series called the Alice Comedies, short films that combined live-action footage with animated images so that human actors appeared to interact with cartoon characters. But he had grown tired of the series and wanted to move on to making completely animated films. In 1927 he got his wish, (4)________ a deal with Universal to produce a new series based on the adventures of a character called Oswald the Lucky Rabbit. Both the name and the species of the character had been picked by Universal—'Oswald' was (5)________ picked out of a hat of names, and the character was made a rabbit because there were already too many cartoon cats on the market.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. empire.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a noun that collocates with "entertainment" to describe a large business built by Walt Disney, on the scale that it is nicknamed the "House of Mouse".

• "Empire" means a large commercial organization or business under the control of one person or group, especially one operating across a wide range of areas. The fixed collocation "entertainment empire" correctly conveys the size and scope of the Disney business described in the passage.

• Applying this to the sentence: "The entertainment empire built by Walt Disney is sometimes called the 'House of Mouse'" fits both the grammar and the meaning of the passage (a vast, multi-faceted entertainment business).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "power" — does not fit the fixed collocation "entertainment ___"; "entertainment power" is not idiomatic in this context.

• Option 3: "province" — means a specific district/area of a country, or a field of activity; it does not describe the scale of a business empire.

• Option 4: "country" — refers to a nation, which is logically incorrect since "entertainment country" makes no sense as a description of a business built by one man.

NOTE

• Common business-scale collocations tested by SSC in cloze passages: "business empire", "media empire", "corporate giant", "conglomerate".

• In cloze passages, always check which option forms a natural, idiomatic collocation with the surrounding words, not just which option is grammatically possible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the sentence "In 1927 he got his wish, ______ a deal with Universal to produce a new series..." — describing the action of finalising/making an agreement with Universal.

• The fixed idiomatic expression is "to strike a deal", meaning to reach an agreement, especially in business. Here it is used in its present participle form "striking" to describe the action happening alongside "he got his wish".

• Applying this to the sentence: "In 1927 he got his wish, striking a deal with Universal to produce a new series..." correctly uses the participial phrase to show that getting his wish and striking the deal happened together.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. apparently.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the sentence "'Oswald' was ______ picked out of a hat of names" — describing how the name Oswald was seemingly/reportedly chosen, based on an account that the passage presents without claiming absolute certainty.

• "Apparently" means as far as one knows or can see; it seems that; reportedly — used to indicate that something is believed to be true based on available information, without asserting it as an established fact.

• Applying this to the sentence: "'Oswald' was apparently picked out of a hat of names" correctly conveys that this is how the naming is reported/believed to have happened, matching the tone of a historical anecdote.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "anatomically" — relates to the structure of the body, entirely unrelated to how a name was chosen.

• Option 3: "reasonably" — means to a fairly acceptable extent, or sensibly; it does not fit the sense of "seemingly/reportedly" required here.

• Option 4: "outwardly" — means on the surface or in outward appearance (as opposed to inner feelings); it does not fit the context of describing how a name was picked.

NOTE

• Adverbs like "apparently", "reportedly", "seemingly", "allegedly" are commonly used in narrative/historical passages to indicate information based on report or appearance rather than confirmed fact — SSC frequently tests the ability to distinguish these from unrelated same-suffix adverbs.

• Distinguish: "apparently" (it seems) vs. "evidently" (it is obvious/proven) — a subtle but sometimes tested distinction.
